6. narrow responsive layout;
7. required operation exposure and invocation path.

The evaluator records unavailable contexts as limitations or inconclusive results; it does not convert missing evaluation into a pass.

## 15.6 Scope boundary

SES-009 defines accessibility-preserving expression rules and evaluation obligations. It does not prescribe a host framework, DOM implementation, ARIA template, or automated accessibility tool.


--- FILE: docs/16-token-asset-resolution.md (73 lines, 4.1 KiB) ---
# 16. Token and Asset Resolution Rules

Status: SES-010

Tokens provide values and Assets provide referenced resources. Resolution is deterministic, typed by category, and separate from host loading or execution.

## 16.1 Token layers and precedence

Token lookup follows this order from broadest to most specific:

```text
primitive -> semantic -> role -> recipe -> explicit expression override -> resolved value
```

An alias resolves recursively through earlier layers only. A later layer may override a value when the target is expression data and the override is declared by the active Theme, Recipe, or explicit expression context. A token may not override semantic identity, operation identity, accessibility relationships, required content, or business behavior.

The final resolved value records its source layer and alias path. Cycles, ambiguous aliases, and undeclared protected-field overrides are failures.

## 16.2 Token rules

- Primitive tokens are raw values without semantic meaning.
- Semantic tokens represent stable interface meaning such as text, surface, status, and interaction.
- Role tokens represent contextual use such as card surface, heading text, or navigation edge.
- Recipe tokens are target-specific aliases and may express visual topology or appearance values.
- Resolved tokens are host-ready values and retain source provenance.
- Components should consume semantic or role aliases rather than Visual Language-specific primitives.
- Missing required tokens fail resolution; optional tokens may use an explicitly declared fallback.
- Fallbacks are not created implicitly for unknown tokens.

## 16.3 Asset categories

Asset IDs resolve within one declared category:

| Category | Examples | Expression use |
|---|---|---|
| fonts | font families and weights | typography |
| icons | symbolic action or status graphics | signaling and ornament |
| images | content or background imagery | media and surfaces |
| textures | paper, grain, material | layered appearance |
| patterns | halftone, grid, motifs | repeated appearance |
| masks | clipping and compositing shapes | appearance construction |
| edges | targeted edge resources | boundary treatment |
| backgrounds | image or generated surface sources | appearance construction |
| ornaments | non-semantic decoration | presentation only |
| custom | host-declared extensions | namespaced expression only |

An asset referenced as one category may not silently resolve from another category. Category aliases require an explicit registry declaration.

## 16.4 Asset rules

- Recipes reference stable Asset IDs, not implicit filesystem discovery.
- The resolver validates identity, category, required metadata, and declared capability before emitting a reference.
- Asset retrieval, decoding, licensing checks, caching, and host capability checks occur outside the pure resolver boundary.
- Missing required assets fail resolution with source path and category evidence.
- Optional decorative assets may be omitted only when the Projection Contract permits omission.
- Custom assets and filters must be namespaced and cannot introduce semantic identity or executable behavior by convention.

## 16.5 Failure codes

- `ERR_TOKEN_UNRESOLVED`: required token or alias has no definition.
- `ERR_TOKEN_CYCLE`: token aliases form a cycle.
- `ERR_TOKEN_AMBIGUOUS`: multiple definitions claim the same precedence position.
- `ERR_PROTECTED_TOKEN_OVERRIDE`: token resolution attempts to mutate a protected semantic field.
- `ERR_ASSET_NOT_FOUND`: required Asset ID is absent.
- `ERR_ASSET_CATEGORY_MISMATCH`: Asset ID exists only under another category.
- `ERR_ASSET_METADATA_INVALID`: required asset metadata is absent or malformed.
- `ERR_ASSET_CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED`: host capability is insufficient for the declared asset use.

Each failure retains the target identity, field path, requested token or Asset ID, category, source layer, and applicable SES-003 check ID.

## 16.6 Scope boundary

SES-010 defines token and Asset resolution semantics only. SES-011 owns full Recipe precedence and conflict handling. This contract does not load files, decode media, execute filters, or implement a host resource provider.


--- FILE: docs/17-recipe-precedence.md (93 lines, 4.1 KiB) ---
# 17. Recipe Precedence and Conflict Handling

Status: SES-011

Recipe resolution combines expression layers without allowing a later expression source to rewrite semantic meaning. Precedence is deterministic, field-specific, and observable in the resolved layer trace.

## 17.1 Precedence order

Layers are applied from lowest to highest precedence:

```text
Visual Language
-> Theme
-> explicit user style options
-> Composition Recipe
-> Socket Recipe
-> Block Recipe
-> Variant Recipe
-> Slot Recipe
-> Element Recipe
-> semantic State Recipe
-> responsive Recipe
-> accessibility overrides
```

The order is fixed for a resolution run. A missing layer is skipped; its absence is not an error unless the Projection Contract marks the layer or field required.

## 17.2 Merge rules

| Value shape | Default merge rule | Conflict behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Scalar expression value | replace at the highest permitted layer | protected or undeclared replacement fails |
| Token alias | replace alias, then resolve | cycle, ambiguity, or protected override fails |
| Object/map | recursively merge declared expression fields | same-precedence incompatible values fail |
| Ordered layer array | append only when the field declares additive semantics | otherwise highest permitted layer replaces the collection |
| Slot presentation map | merge by Slot ID | unknown Slot target fails |
| State/Variant map | merge by declared State or Variant ID | unknown ID fails |
| Protected semantic field | never merge or replace | hard failure |

The default is replacement for scalar fields and replacement for ordered collections unless a field explicitly declares additive semantics. Recipe precedence does not imply that all appearance arrays concatenate.

## 17.3 Protected fields

No Recipe layer may change:

- Element, Block, Slot, Socket, Composition, State, Variant, or Operation identity;
- required content or accepted content type;
- semantic role or accessibility relationship;
- required operation identity or business behavior;
- Projection Contract invariance level;
- routing intent or application data identity.

Such changes are `ERR_PROTECTED_FIELD_OVERRIDE`, even when supplied by an explicit user style option or accessibility override. Accessibility overrides may change expression needed to preserve access; they may not erase the underlying semantic contract.

## 17.4 Conflict policy

1. Resolve layers in the fixed order.
2. Check Projection Contract permission before applying a mutation.
3. Apply the field-specific merge rule.
4. Record source layer, source path, previous value, and resulting value in the layer trace.
5. If two values at the same precedence cannot be merged deterministically, fail with `ERR_RECIPE_CONFLICT`.
6. If a later value targets a protected field, fail with `ERR_PROTECTED_FIELD_OVERRIDE`.
7. If a mutation is not declared by `transform`, `mayOmit`, or `mayIntroduce`, fail with `ERR_TRANSFORM_UNDECLARED` or the applicable projection failure.

No fallback winner is selected for an unresolved conflict. Unknown or ambiguous fields are hard failures rather than silent defaults.

## 17.5 Trace requirements

The resolved expression trace retains, for every changed field:

- semantic target identity;
- field path;
- source layer and Recipe identity;
- prior value, if any;
- resulting value;
- Projection Contract permission;
- merge rule;
- check and evidence identifiers.

This trace supports deterministic replay, conformance evidence, and later change review.

## 17.6 Failure codes

- `ERR_RECIPE_CONFLICT`: incompatible values exist at one precedence level.
- `ERR_PROTECTED_FIELD_OVERRIDE`: a Recipe attempts to mutate semantic or behavioral authority.
- `ERR_TRANSFORM_UNDECLARED`: expression mutation lacks Projection Contract permission.
- `ERR_RECIPE_TARGET_UNKNOWN`: Recipe target cannot be resolved.
- `ERR_RECIPE_LAYER_INVALID`: layer is malformed or not applicable to the target.
- `ERR_RECIPE_MERGE_INVALID`: field value cannot be combined under its declared merge rule.

## 17.7 Scope boundary

SES-011 defines precedence and conflict semantics. It does not implement the resolver, define host styling, or authorize application-specific overrides of semantic authority.


--- FILE: docs/18-semantic-branch-prohibition.md (51 lines, 3.0 KiB) ---
# 18. Semantic Branch Prohibition

Status: SES-012

An implementation must not create Visual Language-specific semantic or business-logic branches. One semantic definition must remain the source for all conforming expressions.

## 18.1 Prohibited branches

The following patterns are non-conforming:

- branching a Block, Slot, Socket, Composition, Operation, or State identity by Visual Language name;
- changing required content, accepted content, operation identity, routing intent, or business behavior by Theme or Recipe;
- maintaining separate language-specific semantic trees that duplicate application logic;
- using decorative variants such as `westernButton`, `edoCard`, or `cyberBadge` as semantic identities;
- hiding or replacing required operations because a Visual Language does not provide a preferred visual treatment;
- embedding Visual Language conditionals in semantic Element or Block behavior when the difference belongs in expression data.

## 18.2 Allowed variation

Expression branches are allowed when they are declarative, target an existing semantic identity, and are governed by a Projection Contract. Permitted variation includes:

- layout topology and morphology;
- typography and token selection;
- media placement and image treatment;
- backgrounds, textures, patterns, edges, masks, bleed, and ornament;
- density, enclosure, alignment, overlap, and responsive arrangement;
- state and operation signaling while preserving exposure and meaning;
- host-specific realization after the renderer-neutral expression boundary.

An expression branch must not add new semantic identity or implicit business behavior. Host extensions are namespaced and remain downstream of canonical SES semantics.

## 18.3 Review checks

- `BRANCH-001`: every semantic target is defined once in the canonical registry.
- `BRANCH-002`: Visual Language and Theme identifiers appear only in expression selection or presentation data.
- `BRANCH-003`: required operations and routing intent are independent of expression selection.
- `BRANCH-004`: language-specific differences are represented by Recipes, tokens, assets, morphology, or appearance.
- `BRANCH-005`: all cross-language vectors use the same semantic fixture and invariant set.
- `BRANCH-006`: host-specific extensions do not redefine canonical semantic fields.

## 18.4 Failure conditions

- `ERR_SEMANTIC_LANGUAGE_BRANCH`: semantic structure changes by Visual Language or Theme.
- `ERR_BUSINESS_LANGUAGE_BRANCH`: business behavior or routing changes by expression selection.
- `ERR_DUPLICATE_SEMANTIC_TREE`: equivalent semantic definitions are forked per language.
- `ERR_OPERATION_LANGUAGE_BRANCH`: required operation identity or exposure depends on language selection.
- `ERR_UNNAMESPACED_HOST_EXTENSION`: host-specific extension enters canonical SES fields without a namespace.

## 18.5 Scope boundary

SES-012 governs architectural review and conformance checks. It does not refactor an implementation, prescribe a programming language, or prohibit legitimate application-level differences that are outside SES expression selection.


--- FILE: docs/19-renderer-neutral-output.md (100 lines, 3.6 KiB) ---
# 19. Renderer-Neutral Output Contract

Status: SES-014

The renderer-neutral output is the boundary product of SES resolution and the input contract for a host renderer. It preserves semantic inspection and required behavior while carrying expression instructions without assuming DOM, CSS, native views, canvas, or a specific framework.

## 19.1 Output sections

Every resolved projection exposes these sections:

```text
identity
semantic
projection
expression
resources
interaction
accessibility
responsive
trace
diagnostics
```

### Identity and semantic

- Composition, Socket, Block, Slot, Element, Variant, and State IDs;
- semantic roles and stable data identities;
- content participation and required/optional status;
- operation identities and required exposure;
- semantic relationships and logical order.

### Projection

- Projection Contract identity and invariance profile;
- preserved, transformed, omitted, and introduced properties;
- applied failure conditions and permitted mutations.

### Expression

- resolved morphology and layout instructions;
- appearance layer instructions;
- typography and image treatment;
- resolved token values or typed token references;
- resolved Asset IDs and category metadata;
- state, variant, and responsive expression decisions;
- motion instructions with reduced-motion alternatives.

### Interaction and accessibility

- operation exposure and signaling metadata;
- enabled/disabled state;
- accessible name, role, relationships, and logical order;
- focus and state-visibility requirements;
- keyboard and reduced-motion obligations.

### Responsive

- active viewport/context;
- applicable responsive rules;
- allowed reorder, collapse, hide, overflow, and reachability behavior;
- required-content and required-operation obligations.

### Trace and diagnostics

- Recipe layer trace;
- token and Asset provenance;
- conformance check references;
- warnings, limitations, and typed failures.

## 19.2 Host neutrality rules

- No output field requires a DOM node, CSS property, React component, native class, canvas primitive, or framework lifecycle.
- Host adapters may map output fields to platform primitives but may not change semantic identity or required operations.
- Host-specific extensions are namespaced and must be declared in the adapter contract.
- Data attributes, ARIA, CSS classes, native accessibility APIs, and event handlers are host realization concerns, not canonical output fields.
- Resource loading and operation invocation remain outside the output contract.

## 19.3 Required invariants

- `OUTPUT-001`: every output semantic identity maps to exactly one source semantic identity.
- `OUTPUT-002`: required content and operation exposure metadata are present.
- `OUTPUT-003`: expression fields are separate from semantic fields.
- `OUTPUT-004`: every resolved token, Asset, and Recipe mutation has provenance.
- `OUTPUT-005`: accessibility and responsive obligations are present even when the host cannot yet realize them.
- `OUTPUT-006`: output is deterministic for the same resolver input.
- `OUTPUT-007`: host extensions cannot overwrite canonical fields.

## 19.4 Failure conditions

- `ERR_OUTPUT_IDENTITY_MISSING`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_REQUIRED_METADATA_MISSING`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_SEMANTIC_EXPRESSION_MIXED`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_PROVENANCE_MISSING`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_ACCESSIBILITY_METADATA_MISSING`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_HOST_EXTENSION_COLLISION`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_UNRESOLVED_RESOURCE`

## 19.5 Scope boundary

SES-014 defines the renderer-neutral output contract only. It does not define a renderer, host adapter, DOM structure, CSS vocabulary, native widget mapping, resource loader, or operation runtime.


--- FILE: docs/20-change-governance.md (74 lines, 3.4 KiB) ---
# 20. Change Governance

Status: SES-015

SES changes are governed by explicit scope, compatibility evidence, conformance impact, and documented authority. A change is not complete merely because a file or schema parses.

## 20.1 Version boundaries

Version independently:

- semantic model and semantic schema;
- expression model and expression schema;
- Projection Contract vocabulary;
- conformance and result schemas;
- resolver and renderer-neutral output contracts;
- Visual Languages and Themes;
- host renderers and downstream implementations;
- transport or synchronization protocols outside SES.

Equal version numbers do not imply compatibility. Each release or draft records which boundaries changed.

## 20.2 Change classes

| Class | Examples | Required review |
|---|---|---|
| Documentation | terminology clarification, examples, non-normative prose | source and vocabulary consistency |
| Additive | new optional field, new expression layer, new fixture | schema compatibility and conformance impact |
| Conformance-tightening | new required check, failure condition, invariant | fixture coverage, migration path, authority review |
| Breaking semantic | identity, Slot, Socket, Operation, state, or required-content change | explicit semantic version change and equivalence review |
| Breaking expression | incompatible output or Recipe contract change | output compatibility and host impact review |
| Deprecation | retiring field, layer, asset category, or rule | replacement, timeline, warning, and removal release |

## 20.3 Required change record

Every normative change records:

- change ID and affected version boundary;
- intent and reason;
- established behavior before the change;
- proposed behavior after the change;
- compatibility class;
- affected schemas, fixtures, validators, resolvers, and host adapters;
- conformance and migration impact;
- evidence and limitations;
- authority and disposition.

## 20.4 Conformance-impact review

Before accepting a normative change, review:

1. SES-001 invariant matrix and affected baseline IDs;
2. positive and negative fixtures;
3. result schema and failure codes;
4. projection-equivalence vectors;
5. responsive and accessibility contracts;
6. resolver and renderer-neutral output contracts;
7. downstream implementation boundary;
8. changelog and deprecation records.

Changes that alter required semantic or behavioral invariants require updated evidence from every affected dependent layer. Missing evidence yields `inconclusive`, not pass.

## 20.5 Deprecation

Deprecation records the deprecated identifier, replacement, first deprecated version, planned removal version or condition, compatibility behavior, and migration evidence. Deprecated semantic identities remain resolvable during the declared compatibility window unless a breaking change is explicitly authorized.

Silent aliases, undocumented removals, and fallback behavior that changes semantic meaning are prohibited.

## 20.6 Changelog requirements

`docs/CHANGELOG.md` records normative changes by version or draft revision. Each entry identifies semantic, expression, schema, conformance, resolver, or implementation-boundary impact. Generated artifacts and local evidence reference the change ID rather than becoming the changelog source of truth.

## 20.7 Scope boundary

SES-015 defines governance and review obligations. It does not assign external release authority, publish packages, modify downstream implementations, or choose a versioning tool.


--- FILE: docs/21-security-trust-boundaries.md (66 lines, 3.6 KiB) ---
# 21. Security and Trust Boundaries

Status: SES-016

SES expression data may control presentation, but it must not silently become executable code, an authority channel, or a path around host security policy. The host decides how untrusted input is loaded, sanitized, sandboxed, and executed.

## 21.1 Trust classes

| Class | Examples | Default treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Declarative data | tokens, layout values, morphology, colors, typography roles, asset IDs | schema validation and bounded resolution |
| Referenced resources | images, fonts, icons, textures, patterns, masks, edge assets | category validation, metadata validation, host policy |
| Constrained custom expression | namespaced custom appearance or host extension | explicit capability declaration, allowlist, isolation, and provenance |
| Executable behavior | scripts, arbitrary code, event handlers, shader code, dynamic imports | outside canonical SES; rejected unless a separately governed host protocol authorizes it |
| Authority-bearing input | navigation target, credential, permission, payment, deployment, persistence command | outside SES expression; never inferred from a Recipe or Asset |

## 21.2 Expression safety rules

- Tokens and Recipes are data, not code.
- Asset IDs resolve through declared registries; arbitrary filesystem or network discovery is not implied.
- Custom sources, filters, blend modes, shaders, and SVG fragments are namespaced and capability-gated by the host.
- A Recipe cannot introduce event handlers, navigation, data mutation, authentication, authorization, persistence, or network requests.
- An Asset cannot create semantic identity, operation identity, accessibility meaning, or business behavior by appearance alone.
- Host adapters validate MIME type, size, dimensions, decoding policy, and supported capabilities before use.
- Remote or user-supplied resources require an external trust and delivery policy; SES records references, not trust.
- Failure is closed: unknown custom types, unsupported capabilities, unsafe references, and malformed metadata fail rather than falling back to execution.

## 21.3 Resource constraints

Hosts define bounded limits for:

- payload size and nesting depth;
- image pixels, animation frames, font tables, and decoded memory;
- filter, mask, blend, and layer complexity;
- custom extension execution time and permissions;
- remote fetch count, origin, protocol, redirect, and timeout policy;
- logging and diagnostic redaction.

SES conformance verifies that a declaration is explicit and typed. Host security policy determines whether the declaration is permitted in a particular environment.

## 21.4 Trust and provenance

Every custom expression, Asset, filter, or host extension retains:

- source identity and category;
- declaring Visual Language, Theme, Recipe, or adapter;
- capability required;
- integrity or version reference when supplied by the host;
- validation and limitation records.

The resolver must not manufacture trust, signatures, authorization, or provenance. Those belong to the delivery or host protocol.

## 21.5 Failure codes

- `ERR_UNTRUSTED_EXECUTABLE_EXPRESSION`
- `ERR_CUSTOM_CAPABILITY_UNDECLARED`
- `ERR_RESOURCE_POLICY_REJECTED`
- `ERR_RESOURCE_METADATA_LIMIT`
- `ERR_RESOURCE_ORIGIN_REJECTED`
- `ERR_HOST_EXTENSION_UNAUTHORIZED`
- `ERR_AUTHORITY_BEHAVIOR_IN_EXPRESSION`
- `ERR_ASSET_DECODE_REJECTED`

## 21.6 Scope boundary

SES-016 defines expression trust boundaries and host obligations. It does not implement sanitization, sandboxing, content security policy, authentication, authorization, remote delivery, signing, or a security adapter.


--- FILE: docs/22-performance-budgets.md (57 lines, 3.0 KiB) ---
# 22. Performance Budgets

Status: SES-017

SES performance budgets bound expression resolution and host handoff without turning the protocol into a renderer-specific benchmark. These are provisional design budgets for a warm, local resolution path; implementations must record actual measurements before claiming qualification.

## 22.1 Baseline budgets

| Surface | Budget | Measurement boundary |
|---|---:|---|
| Pure semantic/expression resolution | 5 ms p95 | resolver entry to renderer-neutral output, excluding resource I/O |
| Token and alias resolution | 1 ms p95 | token lookup and alias expansion, excluding network or disk |
| Asset metadata resolution | 2 ms p95 | registry lookup and metadata validation, excluding decode/fetch |
| Recipe layer count | 12 layers | one output target across the declared cascade |
| Recipe merge depth | 16 nested expression levels | one target resolution |
| Appearance layer count | 32 layers | one resolved target before host realization |
| Responsive recomputation | 8 ms p95 | existing resolved context to changed viewport output, excluding render/layout |
| Motion metadata resolution | 1 ms p95 | state-to-motion instruction selection, excluding playback |
| Renderer-neutral output size | 256 KiB typical target | serialized resolved output excluding external resources |

Budgets are guardrails, not evidence that an implementation meets them. A host may declare a different profile, but it must name the profile, record the rationale, and retain comparable measurements.

## 22.2 Required measurements

Implementations measuring SES performance record:

- semantic target and fixture ID;
- Visual Language, Theme, state, viewport, and accessibility context;
- cold/warm/cache state;
- input size and layer counts;
- p50, p95, and p99 latency where timing is applicable;
- output size and resource counts;
- retries, failures, and budget violations;
- host and runtime conditions;
- limitations and measurement method.

## 22.3 Degradation rules

- Exceeding a budget is a typed performance warning or failure according to the declared profile; it does not authorize semantic simplification.
- Required content, operations, accessibility, and responsive reachability may not be dropped to meet a budget.
- Optional decoration, redundant appearance layers, precomputation, caching, and compilation may be optimized when their Projection Contract permits it.
- Resource fetch or decode time is measured by the host/resource provider, not attributed to pure resolver latency.
- Budget changes are governed changes and require SES-015 review.

## 22.4 Failure codes

- `ERR_RESOLUTION_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_TOKEN_LOOKUP_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_ASSET_METADATA_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_RECIPE_DEPTH_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_APPEARANCE_LAYER_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_RESPONSIVE_RECOMPUTE_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
- `ERR_OUTPUT_SIZE_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`

## 22.5 Scope boundary

SES-017 establishes provisional measurement boundaries and budgets. It does not benchmark a runtime, prescribe hardware, optimize a renderer, or treat unmeasured performance as validated.


--- FILE: docs/23-authoring-boundaries.md (47 lines, 3.9 KiB) ---
# 23. Authoring Boundaries

Status: SES-018

SES authoring remains coherent when each concern is written in its canonical layer. The same fact must not be duplicated across semantic definitions, Recipes, host components, and external protocols with competing authority.

## 23.1 Ownership matrix

| Authoring surface | Owns | Must not own |
|---|---|---|
| Element | atomic semantic role, interaction behavior, accessibility requirements, content requirements | Visual Language identity, topology, theme-specific styling |
| Slot | named content relationship, cardinality, accepted content, priority | coordinates, crop, fixed geometry, visual placement |
| Block | semantic composition, Slots, states, variants, operations, behavior, relationships | theme-specific branches, renderer markup, business transport |
| Socket | typed participation, accepted Blocks, multiplicity, importance, invariants, projection permissions | CSS grid area, pixel coordinates, renderer layout implementation |
| Composition | screen/page semantic organization, hierarchy, priority, participation | fixed pixels, host navigation implementation, transport |
| Projection Contract | preserve/transform/omit/introduce permissions, invariance, failures, required exposure | recipe values, business rules, external authorization |
| Visual Language | graphical grammar, morphology, appearance, typography, image treatment, motion character | semantic identity, operation identity, application data behavior |
| Theme | concrete Visual Language configuration, token overrides, selected Recipe overrides | replacement semantic tree, transport, product navigation |
| Recipe | declarative expression mapping for an existing target, state, variant, responsive context | arbitrary code, semantic branch, ungoverned side effect |
| Token registry | typed values and aliases with provenance | full topology, semantic identity, business behavior |
| Asset registry | stable resource identity, category, metadata, capability declaration | implicit execution, authority, semantic meaning by decoration |
| Resolver | deterministic combination into renderer-neutral output | rendering, loading, operation invocation, persistence |
| Host renderer | platform realization, loading, native accessibility mapping, operation wiring | canonical semantic redefinition, unreviewed behavior changes |
| External protocol/application | transport, persistence, synchronization, auth, business logic, product navigation | redefining SES invariants without an explicit adapter or change record |

## 23.2 Authoring routing rules

1. If a property must remain stable across Visual Languages, author it in the semantic model or Projection Contract.
2. If a property may differ between Visual Languages, author it in Visual Language, Theme, Recipe, Morphology, Appearance, Token, Asset, or Motion data.
3. If a property concerns movement of SES data or resolved expressions, author it in an external protocol.
4. If a property concerns business behavior, persistence, navigation, authorization, or synchronization, author it in the host application or protocol.
5. If a host needs an extension, namespace it and record its capability, provenance, and compatibility boundary.
6. Do not duplicate semantic identity in a renderer component, Theme name, Asset ID, or language-specific variant.

## 23.3 Conflict handling

When two authoring surfaces claim the same field:

- canonical semantic definitions and Projection Contracts govern semantic authority;
- expression layers govern only permitted presentation fields;
- host implementations cannot override canonical output fields;
- external protocols cannot redefine SES meaning by serialization or transport shape;
- unresolved authority is recorded as a conflict, not silently merged.

## 23.4 Scope boundary

SES-018 routes authoring responsibility and authority. It does not reorganize a codebase, choose a repository layout, define a transport schema, or prohibit application concerns outside SES scope.


--- FILE: docs/24-protocol-neutral-adoption.md (74 lines, 4.6 KiB) ---
# 24. Protocol-Neutral Adoption Guidance

Status: SES-020

SES is consumed as a semantic interface representation and governed expression system. An application may use SES without making SES responsible for transport, persistence, synchronization, or product navigation.

## 24.1 Integration boundary

```text
application data and intent
        |
        v
host adapter: map application state to SES semantic input
        |
        v
SES resolver: validate and resolve semantic + expression inputs
        |
        v
renderer adapter: realize renderer-neutral output
        |
        v
host events and operation results
```

The host owns application state, authorization, transport, persistence, synchronization, and navigation. SES owns semantic structure, projection permissions, expression resolution, conformance rules, and renderer-neutral output.

## 24.2 Consumption steps

1. Define or select the SES semantic model: Elements, Slots, Blocks, Sockets, Compositions, Variants, States, and Operations.
2. Declare the Projection Contract, including preserved identities, permitted transformations, omission and introduction rules, constraints, required operations, and failure conditions.
3. Supply content and application state through a host-owned adapter. The adapter maps into SES inputs; it does not move business rules into Recipes or Visual Languages.
4. Select a Visual Language and resolve Theme, Recipe, Morphology, Appearance, Tokens, Assets, Motion, and responsive context through the deterministic resolver boundary.
5. Validate the resolved output and consume it through a renderer adapter for DOM/CSS, native views, or another host platform.
6. Route user operations back to the host through stable operation identity. The host decides authorization, side effects, persistence, and result handling.

## 24.3 Explicit non-responsibilities

| Concern | Owner | SES boundary |
|---|---|---|
| transport and API calls | host application or external protocol | provide data and receive operation outcomes through an adapter |
| persistence and database state | host application | do not store application records or become a system of record |
| synchronization and conflict resolution | host application or external protocol | resolve only the supplied semantic/expression inputs |
| authentication and authorization | host application or external protocol | expose required operation identity; do not infer authority from presentation |
| product navigation | host application | express composition and operation meaning without owning routes |
| rendering | platform renderer adapter | consume renderer-neutral output without redefining semantic meaning |

## 24.4 Adapter rules

- Keep the adapter boundary explicit and versioned.
- Map legacy or application-specific data once at the boundary; downstream SES records use canonical vocabulary.
- Treat unknown semantic discriminators, unsupported capabilities, missing required content, and projection violations as failures.
- Do not branch semantic or business behavior on Visual Language, Theme, Recipe, or renderer identity.
- Keep external protocol payloads separate from canonical SES definitions unless an explicit mapping is recorded.
- Preserve stable semantic and operation identities across all expressions and host renderers.
- Let the host handle retries, idempotency, authorization, and side effects; SES resolution remains pure and local.

## 24.5 Minimal host contract

An adopting application needs only these responsibilities:

| Host responsibility | Required input/output |
|---|---|
| input mapping | application state and intent -> SES semantic input |
| expression selection | approved Visual Language, Theme, Recipe, and context |
| resolution invocation | canonical semantic and expression inputs -> renderer-neutral output |
| rendering | renderer-neutral output -> platform interface |
| operation routing | stable operation identity + host event -> application result |
| lifecycle | validation, logging, retries, persistence, and authorization outside SES |

Adoption is therefore an integration choice, not a transfer of application ownership to SES. A host may adopt only the semantic model, only the resolver contract, or the complete semantic-to-renderer path, provided the declared boundaries and invariants remain intact.

## 24.6 Acceptance boundary

SES-020 is documentation-complete when an adopter can identify the host adapter, resolver, renderer adapter, and operation route; assign transport, persistence, synchronization, authorization, and navigation to the host; and preserve SES semantic identity and projection invariants while changing expression systems.


--- FILE: docs/25-accountability-and-readiness.md (59 lines, 4.6 KiB) ---
# 25. Accountability and Implementation Readiness

Status: Reconciled 2026-08-16; SES-040 candidate qualified locally

This record maps the lessons from the IEPE/SES baseline to canonical artifacts, evidence, limitations, and next authorized work. It distinguishes documented contracts from implemented or empirically validated behavior.

## 25.1 Lesson-to-accountability matrix

| Lesson | Canonical account | Current maturity | Remaining responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| SES is an interface intermediate representation, not a design system | `docs/01-definition.md`, `docs/11-resolver-boundary.md`, `docs/19-renderer-neutral-output.md` | implemented locally | keep runtime APIs renderer-neutral |
| Tokens cannot express all topology changes | `docs/03-expression-model.md`, `docs/17-recipe-precedence.md` | implemented locally | expand morphology coverage without semantic branching |
| Projection Contracts govern expression freedom | `docs/05-projection-contract.md`, `docs/13-projection-equivalence.md` | locally tested | add independent host evaluation |
| Conformance needs evidence, not assertions | `docs/09-conformance-baseline.md`, `docs/10-validator-contract.md`, `docs/conformance/result.schema.json` | locally tested | retain failures and obtain independent evaluator evidence |
| Accessibility and responsiveness are invariants | `docs/14-responsive-invariants.md`, `docs/15-accessibility-expression.md` | metadata locally tested | exercise host-renderer and assistive-technology paths |
| Renderer neutrality is required | `docs/19-renderer-neutral-output.md` | DOM/CSS adapter locally tested | add a second host and compare semantics |
| Host applications own external concerns | `docs/24-protocol-neutral-adoption.md`, `docs/23-authoring-boundaries.md` | adapter boundary locally tested | record each production adapter's authority and version boundary |
| IEPE requires bounded, evidence-backed work | `.iepe/protocol-reference.json`, `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`, `work/GRAPH.md`, `evidence/` | operational layer installed | preserve issue/evidence linkage for implementation work |
| Security and performance precede runtime adoption | `docs/21-security-trust-boundaries.md`, `docs/22-performance-budgets.md` | provisional contracts documented | convert limits and trust checks into executable gates |

## 25.2 Maturity statement

The repository has a **locally qualified implementation candidate** with a documented specification baseline, machine-readable fixtures, result formats, an executable resolver/validator path, a DOM/CSS adapter, local performance measurements, and cross-runtime summary checks. It does not claim production accessibility behavior, production performance, or empirical cross-framework equivalence.

Evidence must promote those dimensions independently:

```text
documented -> implemented -> tested -> empirically validated
```

No later stage may be inferred from an earlier stage's artifact existence.

## 25.3 Responsible implementation gates

Before promoting runtime work beyond the local candidate, the coordinator must require:

1. A pure resolver implementation against `docs/11-resolver-boundary.md` and `docs/19-renderer-neutral-output.md`.
2. A validator implementation that emits `docs/conformance/result.schema.json` records and preserves negative results.
3. At least one host renderer adapter with stable semantic and operation identity.
4. Accessibility and responsive execution evidence from the selected host environment.
5. Security checks for executable expression inputs, unsafe assets, and custom sources.
6. Measurements against provisional budgets, with environment and method recorded before promotion.
7. A framework-neutral adapter test proving application transport, persistence, synchronization, authorization, and navigation remain outside SES.

These are future implementation gates, not claims that the current repository has completed them.

## 25.4 Current material unknowns

- The first host renderer and runtime language are not selected.
- The independent validator implementation boundary is not selected.
- Performance budgets have no empirical calibration environment.
- Accessibility evidence requires a named host platform and evaluator.
- Promotion authority remains `unassigned` in `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`.

These unknowns do not block the specification baseline, but they block implementation-maturity or release-readiness claims.

## 25.5 Next bounded work

SES-040 records the current candidate. The next promotion requires an assigned promotion authority and independent browser/accessibility, production-load, and framework-integration evaluation; those actions remain outside the current local authorization.

# Changelog

## 1.0.0 Draft Standard

- Renamed the umbrella architecture to Semantic Expression System (SES).
- Defined Component as an implementation term rather than an SES semantic layer.
- Added explicit Operation semantics.
- Upgraded Socket to a typed participation and projection boundary.
- Added Projection Contract between semantic structure and expression.
- Added typed invariance for semantic, behavioral, action identity, structural, morphological, and visual properties.
- Added Morphology as a first-class expression layer.
- Replaced atomic surface, edge, texture, and ornament assumptions with layered Appearance Recipes.
- Added full and custom backgrounds, texture layers, pattern layers, targeted edges, multiple edge layers, decoration, masks, clips, bleed, compositing, and z-order support.
- Defined token layers: primitive, semantic, role, recipe, resolved.
- Defined asset registries for fonts, icons, textures, patterns, masks, edges, backgrounds, ornaments, and custom resources.
- Added resolver cascade and host-neutral renderer boundary.
- Added layered conformance and negative fixtures.
- Added independent implementation and protocol boundary for downstream projects such as IV.

--- FILE: docs/README.md (89 lines, 3.3 KiB) ---
# Semantic Expression System

Version: 1.0.0 Draft Standard
Status: Protocol-neutral architecture specification with locally qualified implementation candidate

The Semantic Expression System (SES) is a 2D interface architecture for extreme visual variation without semantic or behavioral fragmentation.

SES separates what an interface means from how it is expressed. Elements, Slots, Blocks, Sockets, Compositions, Variants, States, and Operations define the stable semantic interface representation. Visual Languages, Themes, Recipes, Morphology, Appearance, Tokens, and Assets define replaceable expression. A resolver combines both sides into a concrete rendered interface.

The system is intentionally protocol-neutral and application-neutral. A transport, synchronization, authoring, persistence, or remote rendering protocol can be defined separately. A project such as IV can implement SES without becoming the source of truth for SES itself.

## Governing principle

If a visual decision can reasonably differ between radically different interface languages, it must not be hard-coded into a semantic Element or Block.

Visual variation may include color, typography, geometry, spacing, internal layout, surface construction, background composition, targeted edges, textures, patterns, masks, image treatment, iconography, ornament, density, motion, and responsive presentation.

Semantic identity, data contracts, operation identity, accessibility relationships, required content, state meaning, and business behavior remain governed by the semantic model.

## Architecture

```text
APPLICATION DATA
      |
      v
SEMANTIC INTERFACE REPRESENTATION
  Element
  Slot
  Block
  Socket
  Composition
  Variant
  State
  Operation
      |
      v
PROJECTION CONTRACT
  preserve
  transform
  omit
  introduce
  invariants
  operation exposure
  failure conditions
      |
      v
EXPRESSION SYSTEM
  Visual Language
  Theme
  Recipe
  Morphology
  Appearance
  Tokens
  Assets
      |
      v
RESOLVER / COMPILER
      |
      v
RENDERER
  DOM
  CSS
  native view tree
  other 2D host
```

## Documents

- `01-definition.md` - canonical definition and terminology
- `02-semantic-model.md` - Element, Slot, Block, Socket, Composition, Variant, State, Operation
- `03-expression-model.md` - Visual Language, Theme, Recipe, Morphology, Appearance
- `04-token-system.md` - token layers, aliases, resolution, assets
- `05-projection-contract.md` - preservation and transformation boundary
- `06-runtime-and-rendering.md` - resolver, cascade, DOM contract, compilation
- `07-conformance.md` - validation levels, failure conditions, tests
- `08-implementation-boundary.md` - protocol and IV implementation boundary
- `schemas/ses-schema.ts` - TypeScript canonical schema
- `schemas/ses.schema.json` - JSON Schema interchange draft
- `examples/home-example.ts` - complete semantic and expression example

## Naming

SES is the umbrella architecture.

"Component" is an implementation term, not a semantic layer. A React component can implement an Element, Block, Socket renderer, Composition host, or infrastructure provider.

"Theme" is not the whole expression system. A Theme configures a Visual Language. The Visual Language defines the broader graphical grammar.

"Slot" and "Socket" are intentionally distinct. A Slot receives content inside a Block. A Socket receives compatible Blocks inside a larger semantic structure.


--- FILE: docs/SES-SPECIFICATION.md (850 lines, 21.7 KiB) ---
# 1. Canonical Definition

## 1.1 Semantic Expression System

The Semantic Expression System is a semantic composition architecture in which Elements provide atomic behavior, Slots define named content relationships inside reusable Blocks, Sockets define typed participation boundaries for Blocks inside larger structures, and Compositions define screen-level semantic organization.

Visual Languages provide replaceable graphical grammars. Themes configure those grammars. Recipes map semantic objects to presentation. Morphology controls structural visual organization. Appearance controls layered graphical construction. Tokens and assets provide the resolved values and resources used by the renderer.

A Projection Contract sits between semantic structure and visual expression. It declares which properties must be preserved, which may be transformed, which may be omitted, which presentation-only properties may be introduced, which operations must remain exposed, and which conditions invalidate the projection.

## 1.2 Goal

SES is designed for extreme visual mutation without semantic or behavioral fragmentation.

The same semantic interface may be expressed as a restrained digital product, printed editorial system, dense technical console, handmade paper interface, high-key futurist product, or another visual language without branching into language-specific application screens.

## 1.3 Invariants

The following are semantic by default and should remain stable across Visual Languages unless a contract explicitly permits otherwise:

- semantic role
- data identity
- Block identity
- Slot identity
- Socket identity
- operation identity
- required content
- accessibility relationships
- state meaning
- business behavior
- routing intent
- responsive importance
- content priority

## 1.4 Mutable expression

The following are expression concerns and may vary radically:

- color
- typography
- spacing
- density
- shape
- radius
- clipping
- internal layout
- media placement
- container backgrounds
- layered backgrounds
- custom imagery
- surface material
- targeted edges
- partial edges
- edge imagery
- textures
- patterns
- masks
- blend modes
- ornament
- image treatment
- icon family
- shadow and glow
- section framing
- navigation appearance
- motion
- responsive visual topology

## 1.5 Governing rule

If Neo-Edo, Western Comics, Cybernetic Minimalism, Neo-Capsule Futurism, and MangaVerse Core could reasonably disagree about a visual property, that property belongs in a token, recipe, morphology rule, appearance rule, or Visual Language grammar rather than being hard-coded into a semantic Element or Block.
# 2. Semantic Model

## 2.1 Element

An Element is the smallest semantically meaningful interface object.

Examples include Button, IconButton, Heading, Text, Image, Avatar, Badge, Tag, Input, Select, Checkbox, Switch, Progress, Divider, Rating, and Price.

An Element owns semantics, accessibility, interaction behavior, and content requirements. It should own as little visual identity as possible.

A Button knows that it is actionable and may be primary, destructive, disabled, loading, focused, or pressed. It does not inherently know that it is a pill, ink strip, chrome capsule, square plate, or paper tab.

## 2.2 Slot

A Slot is a named semantic insertion point inside a Block.

A Slot answers: what kind of content belongs here?

Examples include media, title, subtitle, eyebrow, description, leading, trailing, meta, badge, status, actions, footer, overlay, avatar, icon, progress, and price.

A Slot does not prescribe presentation. `slot="media"` means that the content is primary media for the Block. It does not require a specific position, crop, aspect ratio, border, or enclosure.

## 2.3 Block

A Block is a reusable semantic composition of Elements and Slots.

Examples include MediaCard, Hero, Stat, NavigationItem, SearchField, Post, SeriesItem, WorldItem, ActivityItem, SectionHeader, PriceBlock, ProfileSummary, and ProgressSummary.

A Block defines:

- semantic role
- supported Slots
- required and optional content
- semantic ordering
- behaviors
- variants
- states
- operation relationships
- responsive importance
- accessibility relationships

A Block does not completely prescribe its graphical topology.

## 2.4 Socket

A Socket is a named, typed participation boundary within a Block or Composition.

A Socket declares the semantic role of a region, the Blocks it may receive, multiplicity, importance, required operations, invariants, and the transformations permitted during visual projection.

A Slot governs content participation inside a Block. A Socket governs Block participation inside a larger semantic structure.

A Socket is not a coordinate, column, card shell, or CSS grid area. Those are presentation decisions supplied by a Recipe.

A Socket may declare:

- accepted Block identities or capabilities
- single, optional, or repeating participation
- minimum and maximum participants
- content importance
- semantic and behavioral invariants
- structural and morphological freedom
- required operation exposure
- responsive preservation rules
- projection failure conditions

## 2.5 Composition

A Composition is the semantic arrangement and relationship of Sockets for a screen, page, shell, flow, or section.

A Composition defines information hierarchy and participation, not a fixed pixel layout.

A Home Composition might declare Sockets for navigation, utility, hero, statistics, journey, trending, worlds, activity, community, library, closing action, and footer. A Visual Language may render those as rails, panels, printed fields, overlapping editorial regions, or borderless sections while preserving their semantic contracts.

## 2.6 Variant

A Variant is a semantic specialization of an Element or Block.

Examples:

```text
Button
  primary
  secondary
  destructive
  quiet

Card
  default
  featured
  promotional
  interactive

Badge
  status
  category
  live
```

Variants must not encode Visual Language identity. `westernButton`, `edoCard`, and `cyberBadge` are invalid architectural patterns.

## 2.7 State

A State represents interaction or application condition.

Canonical state vocabulary may include:

```text
default
hover
focus
pressed
selected
active
disabled
loading
error
success
warning
read
unread
owned
locked
```

States have stable semantic meaning. The active Visual Language determines how each state is expressed.

## 2.8 Operation

An Operation is a semantic action exposed by the interface.

Examples include open-series, save, purchase, continue-reading, view-all, dismiss, search, submit, and navigate-home.

Operation identity must remain separate from visual signaling. A projection may alter how an operation is signaled, but required operations may not silently disappear because of theme styling.
# 3. Expression Model

## 3.1 Visual Language

A Visual Language is the highest-level 2D graphical grammar in SES.

It defines the coherent rules by which semantic structure is expressed, including palette, typography, spacing, morphology, shape, surface, edge, texture, pattern, image treatment, iconography, depth, ornament, controls, navigation, and motion.

A Visual Language is broader than a palette or conventional design-system theme.

## 3.2 Theme

A Theme is a concrete configuration of a Visual Language.

Example:

```text
Visual Language: Neo-Edo
Themes:
  Neo-Edo / Ink
  Neo-Edo / Vermilion
  Neo-Edo / Moon
  Neo-Edo / Winter
```

A Theme may override tokens and selected Recipes, but should preserve the defining grammar of its Visual Language. If a configuration replaces most of the typography, surface philosophy, shape grammar, image treatment, edge system, morphology, and motion character, it is likely a separate Visual Language.

## 3.3 Recipe

A Recipe maps a semantic target to presentation behavior.

Recipe targets may include:

- Elements
- Blocks
- Sockets
- Compositions
- Slots within Blocks
- States and Variants

A Recipe may define layout, morphology, appearance, typography roles, image treatment, responsive behavior, and state overrides.

Recipes should be declarative data where practical. Theme-specific JSX branches are an anti-pattern.

## 3.4 Morphology

Morphology describes the structural visual organization of an interface independently from its decorative appearance.

Morphology may define:

- hierarchy
- topology
- density
- rhythm
- alignment
- symmetry
- enclosure
- continuity
- direction
- visual weight
- overlap
- fragmentation
- stacking
- grouping

This distinction allows two themes to use identical colors and still differ substantially because their spatial organization, enclosure, rhythm, and hierarchy differ.

## 3.5 Appearance

Appearance is the layered graphical construction of a resolved semantic object.

Appearance must support full and custom construction rather than only flat surface aliases.

An Appearance Recipe may contain:

```text
background layers
surface material
texture layers
pattern layers
edge layers
decoration layers
image treatment
mask
clip
bleed
overflow
blend modes
opacity
z-order
filtering
backdrop effects
```

### Backgrounds

Backgrounds are ordered layers. A container may combine color, gradients, textures, patterns, images, generated artwork, or custom assets.

Backgrounds must be available at Composition, Socket, Block, Slot, and Element levels when the active grammar permits them.

### Textures

Textures describe material character, such as paper fiber, grain, noise, canvas, metal, scratches, ink bleed, or scan artifacts.

### Patterns

Patterns describe intentional repeated graphical structure, such as halftone, screentone, crosshatch, grid, stripes, dots, waves, speedlines, or cultural geometric motifs.

Texture and pattern are separate concepts and may be layered independently.

### Edges

Edges are first-class layered structures rather than simple borders.

An edge layer may target all sides or any subset of top, right, bottom, and left. It may be solid, hairline, double, dashed, ink, brush, deckle, torn, technical, engraved, glowing, embossed, image-based, offset, partial, or custom.

Multiple edge layers may exist simultaneously.

### Decorations

Decorations are non-semantic graphical additions such as seals, brush marks, registration marks, ticks, flourishes, corner graphics, panel numbers, rivets, engraving, or custom illustrations.

Decorations must not create accessibility meaning by themselves.

### Bleed

A Recipe may intentionally allow background, media, edge, or decoration layers to extend beyond a nominal container boundary. Bleed behavior must be explicit and must not obscure required interaction or focus indicators.
# 4. Token System

SES uses a layered token architecture. Tokens provide values. Recipes decide where and how those values are used.

## 4.1 Token levels

```text
Primitive Tokens
      |
Semantic Tokens
      |
Role Tokens
      |
Recipe Tokens
      |
Resolved Tokens
```

## 4.2 Primitive tokens

Primitive tokens are raw values with no interface semantics.

Examples:

```text
color.violet.600
space.4
radius.16
font.outfit
duration.200
shadow.3
```

Semantic components should not consume primitive tokens directly except in low-level infrastructure.

## 4.3 Semantic tokens

Semantic tokens describe stable meaning:

```text
color.canvas
color.surface
color.text.primary
color.text.secondary
color.accent.interaction
color.status.success
color.status.warning
color.status.danger
```

## 4.4 Role tokens

Role tokens describe interface context:

```text
surface.page
surface.navigation
surface.card
surface.card.featured
edge.card
edge.input
edge.navigation
text.heading
text.card.title
space.section
space.card
space.control
```

## 4.5 Recipe tokens

Recipe tokens are aliases introduced for specific semantic targets:

```text
media-card.surface
media-card.edge
media-card.gap
media-card.media.aspect
button.primary.surface
button.primary.edge
button.primary.shape
```

These may be generated or resolved from the active Visual Language and Theme.

## 4.6 Resolved tokens

Resolved tokens are host-ready values emitted after the cascade is complete. In a web renderer they may become CSS custom properties. In another host they may become a typed style object or native resource table.

## 4.7 Assets

A Visual Language may provide an asset registry for:

- fonts
- icons
- textures
- patterns
- masks
- edge images
- background images
- ornaments
- custom illustrations
- SVG fragments
- shaders or filters where supported by the renderer

Recipes reference asset IDs rather than arbitrary file paths when portability matters.

## 4.8 Token rules

1. Components consume semantic or role aliases, not theme-specific raw values.
2. Tokens should not encode full component topology.
3. Recipes may derive aliases from primitives and semantic tokens.
4. Theme overrides must resolve deterministically.
5. Missing required token references are conformance failures.
6. Accessibility overrides have higher precedence than ordinary theme styling.
# 5. Projection Contract

The Projection Contract governs the boundary between semantic structure and visual expression.

It exists to make radical mutation explicit and testable.

## 5.1 Responsibilities

A Projection Contract declares:

- semantic target
- identity and authority
- properties that must be preserved
- properties that may be transformed
- optional properties that may be omitted
- presentation-only properties that may be introduced
- required operations
- required operation exposure
- accessibility constraints
- responsive constraints
- tolerance where applicable
- failure conditions

## 5.2 Typed invariance

Preservation is typed. A projection may be semantically invariant while visually and morphologically different.

Recommended UI invariance dimensions:

```text
semantic
behavioral
actionIdentity
structural
morphological
visual
```

Each may be:

```text
required
bounded
free
```

A typical expressive application may require semantic, behavioral, and action identity invariance while allowing bounded structural change and free morphological and visual change.

## 5.3 Preserve, transform, omit, introduce

Example:

```ts
projection: {
  preserve: [
    "series-identity",
    "content-priority",
    "view-all-operation",
    "accessibility-order"
  ],

  transform: [
    "orientation",
    "media-placement",
    "enclosure",
    "spacing",
    "alignment",
    "surface",
    "edge",
    "texture"
  ],

  mayOmit: [
    "secondary-decoration",
    "nonessential-caption"
  ],

  mayIntroduce: [
    "ornament",
    "background-art",
    "pattern",
    "section-label-decoration"
  ]
}
```

## 5.4 Operation exposure

SES distinguishes operation existence from operation presentation.

At minimum, the runtime should preserve these distinctions:

```text
operation exists
operation is enabled
operation is exposed
operation is signaled
operation is invoked
operation succeeds or fails
```

A Theme may radically alter signaling. It may not silently remove required exposure.

## 5.5 Failure conditions

A projection is invalid if any declared failure condition occurs.

Common failures include:

- required Slot omitted
- required Socket unfilled
- incompatible Block admitted
- required operation unexposed
- focus indicator obscured
- semantic reading order invalidated
- accessibility name lost
- required content clipped or unreachable
- responsive layout violates minimum visibility
- unresolved token or asset reference
- recipe references unknown semantic identity
- theme-specific implementation changes business behavior
# 6. Runtime and Rendering

## 6.1 Resolver

The resolver is the technical center of SES.

Conceptually:

```ts
resolveExpression({
  language,
  theme,
  composition,
  socket,
  block,
  variant,
  slot,
  element,
  state,
  viewport,
  userStyleOptions,
  accessibility
})
```

The resolver produces a deterministic Resolved Expression containing tokens, layout, morphology, appearance, typography, image rules, motion, and host instructions.

## 6.2 Resolution order

Recommended cascade:

```text
Visual Language
      |
Theme
      |
User Style Options
      |
Composition Recipe
      |
Socket Recipe
      |
Block Recipe
      |
Variant Recipe
      |
Slot Recipe
      |
Element Recipe
      |
Semantic State
      |
Responsive State
      |
Accessibility Overrides
```

Later layers may alter expression. They may not rewrite semantic contracts.

## 6.3 Renderer

The renderer realizes the Resolved Expression in a host.

Possible hosts include:

- DOM + CSS
- React Native
- native desktop view trees
- game UI frameworks
- canvas or retained-mode 2D renderers

SES does not require DOM or CSS, though the web is a reference implementation target.

## 6.4 Web DOM contract

A web renderer should keep the semantic structure inspectable.

Example:

```html
<main
  data-composition="home"
  data-language="neo-edo"
  data-theme="vermilion"
>
  <section data-socket="trending" data-importance="primary">
    <article data-block="media-card" data-variant="featured">
      <div data-slot="media"></div>
      <div data-slot="title"></div>
      <div data-slot="meta"></div>
    </article>
  </section>
</main>
```

These attributes are inspection and styling hooks. Accessibility must continue to use correct native semantics and ARIA rather than relying on data attributes.

## 6.5 Compilation

Where possible, static portions of Visual Languages and Themes should be compiled ahead of runtime into:

- CSS variables
- classes
- style sheets
- lookup tables
- asset manifests
- recipe indexes

Runtime resolution should handle state, viewport, instance overrides, and dynamic content without recomputing the entire language.

## 6.6 Component implementation

Component is an implementation category, not an SES semantic level.

A React codebase may contain:

```text
components/elements
components/blocks
components/infrastructure
```

A component implementing an Element or Block should own semantic behavior, accessible structure, event handling, and stable data hooks. Visual Language conditionals should remain outside the component whenever they can be expressed through Recipes and tokens.
# 7. Conformance

SES uses layered conformance. Passing one layer does not imply another.

## S - Semantic Conformance

Checks that Element, Slot, Block, Socket, Composition, Variant, State, and Operation contracts are valid.

Examples:

- required Slots exist
- Socket admission is valid
- required operations are declared
- semantic identity is stable
- accessibility relationships exist

## C - Composition Conformance

Checks hierarchy, content priorities, repetition, responsive importance, and structural constraints.

## R - Recipe Conformance

Checks that every referenced Recipe, token, asset, morphology rule, and appearance rule resolves.

## A - Appearance Conformance

Checks backgrounds, textures, patterns, edges, masks, clipping, bleed, compositing, and decoration for valid construction and renderer support.

## I - Interaction Conformance

Checks keyboard interaction, focus order, focus visibility, operation exposure, disabled states, errors, recovery paths, and state behavior.

## V - Visual Validation

Checks reference renders, intended language fidelity, clipping, overlap, typography, density, and responsive rendering.

Visual validation does not prove semantic or interaction conformance.

## 7.1 Negative fixtures

The test suite should intentionally include invalid languages and themes.

Required negative cases include:

```text
missing required Slot
unknown Block in Socket
required operation hidden
unknown token
unknown asset
invalid edge target
mask covers focus state
background layer references missing source
mobile horizontal overflow
required content clipped
semantic order replaced by decorative order
state variant missing accessibility fallback
```

## 7.2 Language completeness

A language validator should be able to report coverage such as:

```text
Elements covered
Blocks covered
Sockets covered
Compositions covered
Token references valid
Assets valid
Required states covered
Reduced motion covered
High contrast fallback covered
Responsive recipes valid
```

## 7.3 Reference vectors

A project should maintain a small stable set of semantic Compositions rendered through multiple Visual Languages.

For example:

```text
Home + Core
Home + Neo-Edo
Home + Western Comics
Home + Cybernetic Minimalism
```

All must pass the same semantic and operation invariants even when their pixels and morphology differ substantially.
# 8. Protocol and Implementation Boundary

SES defines interface semantics and expression. It intentionally does not define a transport or synchronization protocol.

A separate protocol may define how SES definitions, instances, assets, state changes, or resolved expressions move between processes, repositories, tools, runtimes, or devices.

## 8.1 SES owns

- canonical semantic types
- Slot and Socket contracts
- Block and Composition definitions
- Visual Language structure
- Theme structure
- Recipe model
- Morphology model
- Appearance model
- token semantics
- asset references
- projection contracts
- resolver semantics
- conformance rules

## 8.2 A separate protocol may own

- serialization format
- transport
- remote references
- capability negotiation
- version negotiation
- patching and deltas
- persistence
- synchronization
- authoring messages
- asset delivery
- cache policy
- signatures
- authentication and authorization

## 8.3 IV implementation boundary

IV should be treated as a downstream implementation of SES, not the definition of SES.

The recommended relationship is:

```text
SES Specification
      |
SES Protocol
      |
IV Adapter / Runtime
      |
IV Components and Screens
```

The implementation may expose optimizations or host-specific extensions, but those extensions should be namespaced and must not silently redefine canonical SES semantics.

## 8.4 Versioning

Version independently:

```text
SES semantic schema
SES expression schema
SES protocol
Visual Languages
Themes
Renderer
IV implementation
```

Equal version numbers do not imply compatibility. Compatibility should be declared explicitly.

import type {
  BlockDefinition,
  CompositionDefinition,
  ExpressionRecipe,
  VisualLanguage,
} from "../schemas/ses-schema";

export const MediaCard: BlockDefinition = {
  id: "media-card",
  name: "Media Card",
  kind: "content",
  semanticRole: "media-content-summary",
  states: ["default", "hover", "focus", "selected", "disabled"],
  operations: ["open-media"],
  slots: [
    { id: "media", name: "Media", semanticRole: "media", cardinality: "one", content: { type: "element", accepts: ["image"] } },
    { id: "badge", name: "Badge", semanticRole: "annotation", cardinality: "optional", content: { type: "element", accepts: ["badge"] } },
    { id: "title", name: "Title", semanticRole: "title", cardinality: "one", content: { type: "element", accepts: ["heading", "label"] } },
    { id: "subtitle", name: "Subtitle", semanticRole: "subtitle", cardinality: "optional", content: { type: "element", accepts: ["text", "label"] } },
    { id: "meta", name: "Meta", semanticRole: "meta", cardinality: "optional", content: { type: "any" } },
    { id: "action", name: "Action", semanticRole: "action", cardinality: "optional", content: { type: "element", accepts: ["button", "icon-button"] } },
  ],
  behavior: { interactive: true, navigable: true },
};

  id: "home",
  name: "Home",
  type: "screen",
  sockets: [
    {
      id: "home.hero",
      name: "Hero",
      semanticRole: "primary-introduction",
      accepts: ["hero"],
      multiplicity: "single",
      importance: "primary",
      invariance: {
        semantic: "required",
        behavioral: "required",
        actionIdentity: "required",
        structural: "bounded",
        morphological: "free",
        visual: "free",
      },
      projection: {
        preserve: ["identity", "primary-action", "accessibility-order"],
        transform: ["orientation", "media-placement", "enclosure", "background", "edges", "texture", "pattern", "ornament"],
        mayIntroduce: ["decorative-art", "background-art"],
        failureConditions: ["primary-action-unexposed", "required-content-unreachable"],
      },
      operations: {
        required: ["enter-world"],
        requireExposure: true,
      },
    },
    {
      id: "home.trending",
      name: "Trending",
      semanticRole: "content-discovery",
      accepts: ["media-rail", "media-grid", "ranked-collection"],
      multiplicity: "single",
      importance: "primary",
      invariance: {
        semantic: "required",
        behavioral: "required",
        actionIdentity: "required",
        structural: "bounded",
        morphological: "free",
        visual: "free",
      },
      projection: {
        preserve: ["content-identity", "content-priority", "view-all-operation"],
        transform: ["orientation", "card-topology", "spacing", "alignment", "enclosure"],
        mayIntroduce: ["texture", "pattern", "section-decoration"],
      },
      operations: {
        required: ["open-media", "view-all"],
        requireExposure: true,
      },

  ],
};

export const NeoEdoMediaCard: ExpressionRecipe = {
  layout: {

## SUBSYSTEM: CANONICAL CONTRACT SCHEMAS & PROTOCOL DEFINITIONS (2 files)

--- FILE: docs/schemas/ses-schema.ts (322 lines, 7.8 KiB) ---
export type ID = string;
export type TokenRef = `--${string}` | `{${string}}` | string;

export type SemanticState =
  | "default" | "hover" | "focus" | "pressed" | "selected" | "active"
  | "disabled" | "loading" | "error" | "success" | "warning"
  | "read" | "unread" | "owned" | "locked" | string;

export type InvarianceRequirement = "required" | "bounded" | "free";

export interface ElementDefinition {
  id: ID;
  kind: string;
  role?: string;
  variants?: string[];
  states?: SemanticState[];
  operations?: ID[];
  accessibility?: {
    role?: string;
    labelRequired?: boolean;
    keyboardInteractive?: boolean;
  };
}

export interface SlotDefinition {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  semanticRole: string;
  cardinality: "one" | "optional" | "many";
  content:
    | { type: "element"; accepts?: ID[] }
    | { type: "block"; accepts?: ID[] }
    | { type: "content"; accepts?: string[] }
    | { type: "any" };
  priority?: number;
  fallback?: unknown;
}

export interface BlockDefinition {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  kind: string;
  semanticRole: string;
  slots: SlotDefinition[];
  variants?: string[];
  states?: SemanticState[];
  operations?: ID[];
  behavior?: {
    interactive?: boolean;
    selectable?: boolean;
    navigable?: boolean;
    expandable?: boolean;
    dismissible?: boolean;
  };
  constraints?: {
    requiredSlots?: ID[];
    mutuallyExclusiveSlots?: ID[][];
    minItems?: number;
    maxItems?: number;
  };
}

export interface SocketAcceptedBlock {
  block: ID;
  variants?: string[];
  capabilities?: string[];
}

export interface InvarianceProfile {
  semantic?: InvarianceRequirement;
  behavioral?: InvarianceRequirement;
  actionIdentity?: InvarianceRequirement;
  structural?: InvarianceRequirement;
  morphological?: InvarianceRequirement;
  visual?: InvarianceRequirement;
}

export interface ProjectionContract {
  preserve?: string[];
  transform?: string[];
  mayOmit?: string[];
  mayIntroduce?: string[];
  failureConditions?: string[];
  tolerance?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export interface OperationContract {
  required?: ID[];
  optional?: ID[];
  requireExposure?: boolean;
  requireSignaling?: boolean;
}

export interface SocketDefinition {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  semanticRole: string;
  accepts: Array<ID | SocketAcceptedBlock>;
  multiplicity: "single" | "optional" | "repeat";
  importance?: "primary" | "secondary" | "tertiary";
  order?: number;
  constraints?: {
    min?: number;
    max?: number;
    preferredSpan?: "narrow" | "medium" | "wide" | "full";
    overflow?: "wrap" | "scroll" | "clip" | "paginate" | "none";
    required?: boolean;
  };
  invariance?: InvarianceProfile;
  projection?: ProjectionContract;
  operations?: OperationContract;
  responsive?: {
    priority?: number;
    collapseInto?: ID;
    hideBelow?: string;
    reorderAllowed?: boolean;
    preserveRequiredOperations?: boolean;
  };
}

export interface CompositionDefinition {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  type: "screen" | "page" | "flow" | "shell" | "section";
  sockets: SocketDefinition[];
  hierarchy?: CompositionNode[];
}

export interface CompositionNode {
  socket: ID;
  children?: CompositionNode[];
  relation?: "sequence" | "group" | "parallel" | "aside" | "overlay";
  priority?: number;
}

export interface MorphologyRecipe {
  hierarchy?: string;
  topology?: string;
  density?: string;
  rhythm?: string;
  alignment?: string;
  symmetry?: string;
  enclosure?: string;
  continuity?: string;
  direction?: string;
  overlap?: string;
  fragmentation?: string;
  visualWeight?: Record<string, number>;
}

export type BackgroundLayer =
  | { type: "color"; value: string; opacity?: number; blendMode?: string }
  | { type: "gradient"; value: string; opacity?: number; blendMode?: string }
  | { type: "texture"; source: ID; opacity?: number; blendMode?: string; mask?: string }
  | { type: "pattern"; source: ID; opacity?: number; blendMode?: string; mask?: string }
  | { type: "image"; source: ID; fit?: string; position?: string; opacity?: number; blendMode?: string }
  | { type: "custom"; source: ID; props?: Record<string, unknown> };

export interface EdgeLayer {
  sides: "all" | Array<"top" | "right" | "bottom" | "left">;
  style: string;
  width?: string;
  color?: string;
  opacity?: number;
  source?: ID;
  offset?: string;
  inset?: boolean;
  start?: string;
  end?: string;
  repeat?: "stretch" | "repeat" | "round";
  mask?: string;
}

export interface TextureLayer {
  source: ID;
  opacity?: number;
  blendMode?: string;
  scale?: string | number;
  direction?: string;
  mask?: string;
}

export interface PatternLayer {
  source: ID;
  placement?: string;
  opacity?: number;
  blendMode?: string;
  scale?: string | number;
  rotation?: number;
  density?: number;
  mask?: string;
}

export interface DecorationLayer {
  id?: ID;
  type: string;
  source?: ID;
  anchor?: string;
  x?: string;
  y?: string;
  width?: string;
  height?: string;
  rotation?: number;
  opacity?: number;
  blendMode?: string;
  zIndex?: number;
  bleed?: Partial<Record<"top" | "right" | "bottom" | "left", string>>;
}

export interface AppearanceRecipe {
  background?: BackgroundLayer[];
  textures?: TextureLayer[];
  patterns?: PatternLayer[];
  edges?: EdgeLayer[];
  decorations?: DecorationLayer[];
  mask?: string | Record<string, unknown>;
  clip?: string | Record<string, unknown>;
  bleed?: Partial<Record<"top" | "right" | "bottom" | "left", string>>;
  overflow?: "visible" | "hidden" | "clip";
  opacity?: number;
  blendMode?: string;
  filter?: string;
  backdrop?: string;
}

export interface LayoutRecipe {
  display?: "block" | "flex" | "grid" | "overlay" | string;
  flow?: string;
  columns?: string;
  rows?: string;
  areas?: string[];
  align?: string;
  justify?: string;
  gap?: string;
  padding?: string;
  margin?: string;
  aspectRatio?: string;
  overflow?: string;
  position?: string;
  transform?: string;
}

export interface SlotPresentationRecipe {
  placement?: string;
  order?: number;
  gridArea?: string;
  width?: string;
  height?: string;
  margin?: string;
  padding?: string;
  typography?: ID;
  image?: ID;
  appearance?: AppearanceRecipe;
  visibility?: string;
}

export interface ExpressionRecipe {
  layout?: LayoutRecipe;
  morphology?: MorphologyRecipe;
  appearance?: AppearanceRecipe;
  typography?: ID | Record<string, ID>;
  image?: ID;
  slots?: Record<ID, SlotPresentationRecipe>;
  state?: Record<SemanticState, Partial<ExpressionRecipe>>;
  variants?: Record<string, Partial<ExpressionRecipe>>;
  responsive?: Record<string, Partial<ExpressionRecipe>>;
}

export interface TokenRegistry {
  primitives?: Record<string, string | number>;
  semantic?: Record<string, string | number>;
  roles?: Record<string, string | number>;
}

export interface AssetRegistry {
  fonts?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  icons?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  textures?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  patterns?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  masks?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  edges?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  backgrounds?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  ornaments?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  images?: Record<ID, unknown>;
  custom?: Record<ID, unknown>;
}

export interface VisualLanguage {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  description?: string;
  philosophy?: string;
  defaultTheme: ID;
  tokens: TokenRegistry;
  assets?: AssetRegistry;
  foundations?: Record<string, unknown>;
  recipes: {
    elements?: Record<ID, ExpressionRecipe>;
    blocks?: Record<ID, ExpressionRecipe>;
    sockets?: Record<ID, ExpressionRecipe>;
    compositions?: Record<ID, ExpressionRecipe>;
  };
}

export interface ThemeDefinition {
  id: ID;
  name: string;
  language: ID;
  mode?: string;
  tokenOverrides?: Record<string, string | number>;
  assetOverrides?: Partial<AssetRegistry>;
  recipeOverrides?: VisualLanguage["recipes"];
}

export interface UIExpressionState {
  visualLanguage: ID;
  theme: ID;
  styleOptions?: Record<string, unknown>;
  viewport?: string;
  reducedMotion?: boolean;
  highContrast?: boolean;
}
